title: “THIS IS THE DAY THE LORD HAS MADE” — YOU WERE PROBABLY NEVER TOLD WHAT PSALM 118:24 COMES AFTER
paragraphs: “THIS IS THE DAY THE LORD HAS MADE” — YOU WERE PROBABLY NEVER TOLD WHAT PSALM 118:24 COMES AFTER

We quote it when the sun rises. We print it on coffee mugs. We post it over beautiful mornings. But Psalm 118:24 is surrounded by rejection, desperate cries for salvation, a rejected stone, and a stunning reversal only God could accomplish. And once you see the bigger story, “this is the day” may never sound ordinary again.
There are Bible verses we know so well that we can stop hearing them.
Psalm 118:24 may be one of them.
“This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.”
You may have whispered it while opening the curtains in the morning.
You may have posted it beneath a sunrise.
Maybe you have repeated it on a day when you desperately needed to convince your own heart that life was still worth facing.
And there is nothing wrong with thanking God for another day.
Every heartbeat is evidence that God has permitted us another moment beneath His heaven.
But Psalm 118:24 has a larger story.
And that story becomes far more powerful when you stop isolating verse 24 and begin listening to what happens immediately before it.
זֶה־הַיּוֹם עָשָׂה יְהוָה נָגִילָה וְנִשְׂמְחָה בוֹ
Zeh-hayyom asah YHWH; nagilah venismechah vo.
“This is the day the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”
Because just before the psalmist announces that there is a day God has made, something has been rejected.
“The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.”
“This is the LORD'S doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.”
“This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.”
What human builders looked at and considered unsuitable, God chose for a place of astonishing importance.
And the psalmist looks at this reversal and essentially declares:
And suddenly verse 24 no longer sounds like nothing more than a cheerful sentence about waking up on Tuesday morning.
There is a rejected stone behind it.
And for Christians, the story becomes even more breathtaking because Jesus Himself reached into this psalm and applied the rejected-stone imagery in His teaching.
The apostles later used the same rejected-stone language concerning Christ in Acts 4:11.
The New Testament does not leave Christians guessing about the ultimate Christ-centered significance it sees in that rejected stone.
Jesus Christ—the One despised, rejected, condemned, crucified and treated as though He could simply be removed—became the cornerstone.
The verdict of men was not the verdict of God.
That changes the emotional weight of this psalm.
Because perhaps you know something about rejection too.
Maybe somebody looked at your worst chapter and decided that chapter was your entire identity.
Maybe people know what you did ten years ago but have no idea what Jesus has been doing inside you since.
Maybe you disappointed people who trusted you.
Maybe you carry memories you wish could be burned from history.

Maybe there are things in your browser history, your private conversations, your relationships, your finances, your thoughts, your past, or your secret life that you would be terrified to see projected onto a church screen.
And sometimes the cruelest builder rejecting the stone is the person staring back at you in the mirror.
You know what nobody else knows.
So when someone tells you that God can redeem your story, part of you wants to believe it...
But look again at the stone.
What looked finished was not finished.
And here is where we must be careful.
Psalm 118 is not promising that every rejection in your life will result in earthly fame.
It is not saying everyone who walked away will come crawling back.
It is not promising that God will make everybody who hurt you regret what they did.
The Gospel gives us something infinitely greater.
It tells us that human rejection cannot overturn the purposes of God.
And nowhere is that more gloriously visible than in Jesus Christ.
The cross looked like rejection at its most brutal.
His followers watched their expectations collapse beneath the weight of a cross.
That is the heartbeat Christians hear when the New Testament reaches back to Psalm 118 and identifies Jesus with the rejected stone.
But the builders did not have the final word.
Neither does the ugliest thing you have confessed at two in the morning with tears running down your face.
Grace is not permission to continue comfortably in rebellion.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could decorate our chains with Christian vocabulary.
To call us out of darkness and into His light.
That means the Gospel does not tell you to pretend your sin never happened.
your sin does not have to write the final sentence.
That is why our message has always been:
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored.
But because in Christ, guilt can meet forgiveness.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
And sinners who deserve judgment can discover that the Son of God willingly stood in the place of sinners.
But there is another detail hiding just a few verses later.
That cry matters because Psalm 118:26 immediately says:
“Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD.”
When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds drew from this very psalm.
“Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.”
A psalm containing the cry for salvation...
the coming One in the name of the LORD...
“This is the day which the LORD hath made.”
And then the Gospel narratives bring language from that psalm onto the streets surrounding Jesus.
This is why we cannot live on isolated Bible quotations while ignoring the story surrounding them.
“This is the day” belongs to a song saturated with deliverance, thanksgiving, reversal, worship and salvation.
For Christians reading Psalm 118 in the light of the New Testament, its rejected-stone imagery leads directly toward Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs today.
Because you woke up this morning...
but something inside you did not want to.
You smiled at people while quietly falling apart.
Nobody noticed that there was a war happening behind your eyes.
Maybe what you need today is not another motivational sentence telling you to “stay positive.”
Maybe you need something stronger than positivity.
Because there comes a point when motivational quotes cannot reach the places sin has wounded.
There comes a point when self-improvement cannot resurrect a dead heart.
There comes a point when pretending becomes exhausting.
And still carry the same unhealed, unconfessed, unforgiven weight into every new room.
Jesus does not merely offer a better morning.
And perhaps “this is the day” needs to become personal for you in an entirely different way.
Maybe this is the day you stop running.
Maybe this is the day you confess what you have spent years defending.
Maybe this is the day you stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Maybe this is the day you forgive because Christ forgave you.
Maybe this is the day you finally admit that religion cannot save you.
Maybe this is the day you stop trying to impress God with a cleaned-up version of yourself and fall before Christ with empty hands.
Maybe this is the day you whisper:
Not because the calendar possesses magical power.
Not because Psalm 118:24 guarantees that everything you want will happen today.
But because Scripture repeatedly confronts us with the urgency of responding to God rather than endlessly postponing repentance.
You are not promised unlimited tomorrows.
And perhaps the most dangerous word in your spiritual vocabulary is not “never.”
I’ll come back to God later.
I’ll deal with that sin later.
But grace is standing before you now.
There is no shame in admitting that you need grace.
The church was never supposed to be a museum of people who successfully rescued themselves.
We are people whose only hope is Jesus.
And somebody reading the comments may discover that they are not the only one fighting.
Your honesty may become the doorway through which another wounded believer finally stops pretending.
don’t let this article die on your screen.
If someone came to your mind while reading this, there may be a reason.
Simply because sometimes people are carrying battles they never announce.
They may never search for a sermon.
They may never tell you they are struggling.
Long enough to hear about Jesus.
Long enough to remember that grace is still calling.
But God can use a simple act of faithfulness in ways you may never see.
Not because every day will feel victorious.
When your past starts introducing itself again.
The cross was not evidence that God had lost control.
The resurrection was not an emergency repair to a plan gone wrong.
If Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, grow in Christ, and remember the Gospel when life becomes unbearably loud, stay close.

And there is another way you can help this work continue.
Not because giving can purchase salvation.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ, not a product anyone can sell.
But Christians are called to generosity, and voluntary financial support can genuinely help Gospel-centered work continue.
So if you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior keep creating, publishing, reaching, teaching, and expanding?”
Never because you think God owes you something afterward.
And never beyond what you can responsibly give.
But whether you ever spend a single cent with us or not...
Christ paid the price sinners could never pay.
That is why financial support should flow from gratitude and willing partnership—not fear, guilt, spiritual pressure, or an attempt to purchase God's blessing.
Put truth into somebody else's feed.
Sometimes the person who cannot give money can still carry the message farther than money ever could.
And perhaps that brings us back to where we began.
“This is the day which the LORD hath made.”
You may have read those words hundreds of times.
But perhaps now you will hear the footsteps surrounding them.
“Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD.”
And through the New Testament, the rejected Stone has a name.
So tomorrow morning, when sunlight reaches your window and Psalm 118:24 comes to mind, thank God for another day.
But remember that the verse belongs to something much bigger than beautiful weather.
Remember the God who overturns human verdicts.
And when your past tells you that your scandal is the end of your story, do not let shame hold the pen that belongs in the hands of your Redeemer.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Walk away from the darkness you once protected.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people congratulating themselves for having clean histories.
It is the story of sinners who desperately needed a Savior...
and discovered that the Stone the builders rejected became the cornerstone.
Your support can help us keep going.
Your share can help carry the message somewhere we cannot personally go.
Your comment may encourage somebody who thought they were fighting alone.
Your prayer matters more than analytics can measure.
But never forget the center of all of it.
The only One who can take a sinner's confession, a shattered history, a ruined reputation, a prodigal heart, a life buried beneath shame...
and write something grace alone could have written.
The stone they rejected was not the end of the story—and neither is the chapter of your life that made you think God could never use you again.
